section.title: Abraham Pleads for Sodom
section.sectionRationale: Having confirmed the promise, the LORD lets Abraham in on His purpose to judge Sodom, treating him as a friend and a chosen intercessor for the nations. Abraham's bold, humble bargaining probes the justice and mercy of God and models intercession that appeals to God's own righteousness.
section.thesis: The Judge of all the earth invites His chosen friend to plead, and Abraham intercedes for the wicked on the ground of the righteous few, learning that God will spare a whole city for the sake of a remnant and will always do what is right.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the LORD resolves to disclose His purpose to Abraham; and Abraham's descending appeal from fifty to ten righteous ones.

units.label: Shall I hide from Abraham?
units.note: the LORD confides in His friend

verses.text: When the men got up to leave, they looked out over Sodom, and Abraham walked along with them to see them off.
And the LORD said, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
Abraham will surely become a great and powerful nation, and through him all the nations of the earth will be blessed.

For I have chosen him, so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just, in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what He has promised.”
Then the LORD said, “The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great. Because their sin is so grievous,
I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry that has reached Me. If not, I will find out.”

units.label: Will not the Judge do right?

verses.text: And the two men turned away and went toward Sodom, but Abraham remained standing before the LORD.
Abraham stepped forward and said, “Will You really sweep away the {{tsaddiq|righteous}} with the wicked?
What if there are fifty righteous ones in the city? Will You really sweep it away and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous ones who are there?

{{chalilah|Far be it}} from You to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous and the wicked are treated alike. Far be it from You! Will not the {{shaphat|Judge}} of all the earth do what is right?”
So the LORD replied, “If I find fifty righteous ones within the city of Sodom, on their account I will spare the whole place.”
Then Abraham answered, “Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes,
suppose the fifty righteous ones lack five. Will You destroy the whole city for the lack of five?” He replied, “If I find forty-five there, I will not destroy it.”
Once again Abraham spoke to the LORD, “Suppose forty are found there?” He answered, “On account of the forty, I will not do it.”
Then Abraham said, “May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak further. Suppose thirty are found there?” He replied, “If I find thirty there, I will not do it.”
And Abraham said, “Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, suppose twenty are found there?” He answered, “On account of the twenty, I will not destroy it.”
Finally, Abraham said, “May the Lord not be angry, but let me speak once more. Suppose ten are found there?” And He answered, “On account of the ten, I will not destroy it.”
When the LORD had finished speaking with Abraham, He departed, and Abraham returned home.

tsaddiq.gloss: Righteous, just, in the right. Abraham's whole plea turns on the presence of the righteous within a wicked city, and on whether God will treat them the same as the guilty. The word raises the question of how the just and the unjust can be dealt with rightly.

chalilah.gloss: Far be it, an expression of horror at something unthinkable, almost profane. Abraham uses it twice, appealing to God's own character: it would be unthinkable for the righteous Judge to slay the righteous with the wicked. He argues with God on the basis of who God is.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, govern, decide, vindicate. The Judge of all the earth is the ruler who alone has the right and wisdom to condemn and to acquit. Abraham's confidence rests on the certainty that this Judge will do what is right, that His justice can be trusted.

basic.context: As the visitors head toward Sodom, the LORD chooses to tell Abraham what He is about to do, treating him as a friend and as the one through whom the nations will be blessed. Abraham then pleads for the city. The key question is out loud in verse 25: will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real conversation, and it teaches us how to intercede: boldly yet humbly, appealing to God's own character. The main point is God's perfect justice joined to His readiness to spare for the sake of the righteous. Readers ask whether Abraham changed God's mind or was drawn into God's own heart, but either way God's justice is vindicated.
basic.originalLanguages: The whole plea turns on the righteous, the tsaddiq, and whether they will be swept away with the wicked. Abraham twice cries chalilah, far be it, an appeal to God's character. He trusts the shaphat, the Judge of all the earth, to do right. His argument is not against God's justice but from it.
basic.typology: God's willingness to spare the many for the sake of a righteous few points forward to the one righteous One, Christ, for whose sake a whole people is spared. Abraham standing before the LORD to plead prefigures the great Intercessor.
basic.christ: Where ten righteous could not be found in Sodom, God provides one perfectly righteous Man, Jesus, and for His sake spares all who are His. Christ is the Intercessor who ever lives to plead for His people, greater than Abraham.
basic.god: God is perfectly just, never treating the righteous and the wicked alike, and He is merciful, ready to spare a whole city for a remnant. He is humble enough to confide in a friend and to be pleaded with.
basic.crossReferences: James calls Abraham the friend of God. Ezekiel 22 has God seeking one to stand in the gap. Romans 5 shows how the righteousness of one brings life to many.
basic.oneStory: Here God reveals His justice and His mercy together and invites His friend to intercede. The pattern of sparing the many for the righteous few reaches its fulfillment in Christ, the one righteous One for whose sake God spares a countless people from judgment.

context.literary:
The passage is the hinge between the meal at Mamre and the fire on Sodom. It opens with a look: the men "looked out over Sodom," verse 16. Chapter 19 closes the same unit with Abraham returning to the spot and looking down "toward Sodom and Gomorrah," Genesis 19:28, the same verb in Hebrew. Between those two looks lies everything Abraham asked and everything God did.

The first movement, verses 17 to 21, is a divine soliloquy. The reader overhears God deliberating with Himself, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" This is rare in Genesis, and its effect is to let the reader into the reason for the conversation before it happens. God's reasons are drawn from the covenant: Abraham will become a great nation, the nations will be blessed through him, verse 18, and he has been chosen to teach his household "the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just," verse 19. Then comes the news about Sodom, framed in legal language: an outcry, an investigation, a finding, verses 20 and 21.

The second movement, verses 22 to 33, is a dialogue built on strict repetition with variation. Abraham speaks six times, and God answers six times. The numbers fall from fifty to forty-five, then to forty, thirty, twenty and ten. Each time Abraham's preface grows more deferential: "Now that I have ventured to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes," verse 27; "May the Lord not be angry," verse 30; "let me speak once more," verse 32. God's replies stay short and unchanging in substance: I will not destroy it. The contrast is deliberate. Abraham's anxiety grows with every step, while God's readiness to spare never wavers.

The passage is framed by movement. It begins with the men getting up to leave and Abraham walking along to see them off, verse 16, and it ends with the LORD departing and Abraham returning home, verse 33. In between, Abraham "remained standing before the LORD," verse 22. The next chapter will begin with the other two arriving at Sodom in the evening, and the reader goes into it knowing exactly what God has promised about ten righteous people.
context.historical:
From the hills near Hebron the land falls steeply east toward the Dead Sea basin, and the plain of the cities lay below. Abraham could see the smoke of Sodom from where he had stood, Genesis 19:28. The cities had long been in the story. Lot had chosen the well watered plain and "pitched his tent toward Sodom," though "the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD," Genesis 13:10-13. Abraham had once rescued Lot and the people of Sodom from invading kings, Genesis 14:14-16, and refused to take so much as a thread from the king of Sodom, Genesis 14:22-23. He knew the city, and he had a nephew inside it.

The "outcry" of verses 20 and 21 is a legal and social term. It is the cry of the oppressed calling for justice, the word used when Israel cried out under Egyptian oppression, Exodus 3:7 and 3:9, and when the law warns that the widow and orphan who are mistreated will "cry out to Me in distress," Exodus 22:23. Abel's blood "cries out" from the ground, Genesis 4:10. God hears such cries as a judge hears a complaint. His "I will go down to see" is the language of a judge who investigates before sentencing.

Abraham's plea assumes a way of thinking common in the ancient world, that a city stood or fell as a whole. The righteous inside Sodom would share the fate of the wicked unless God distinguished them. Later law would insist that each person dies for his own sin, Deuteronomy 24:16, and Ezekiel would press the same point, Ezekiel 18:20. Abraham does not ask God to separate the righteous from the city. He asks something bolder: that the presence of the righteous should protect the whole place.

For Israel, the scene gave a picture of what their ancestor had been chosen for. He was to be the channel of blessing to the nations, Genesis 12:3, and here he stands before God on behalf of a Canaanite city with no claim on him but his nephew and his compassion.
context.canonical:
This is the first sustained intercession in the Bible, and it sets the pattern for Israel's mediators. Abraham himself will pray for Abimelech, and God will call him "a prophet" who "will pray for you," Genesis 20:7 and 20:17. Moses stands between God and Israel after the golden calf, Exodus 32:11-14 and 32:32, and after Kadesh, Numbers 14:19-20. Psalm 106:23 remembers that Moses "stood before Him in the breach," the same posture as Abraham who "remained standing before the LORD." Moses and Aaron ask a question much like Abraham's: "when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?" Numbers 16:22. Samuel says, "far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you," 1 Samuel 12:23, using Abraham's own exclamation.

The prophets pick up the logic of the righteous few. Jeremiah is told to search Jerusalem's streets for "a single person" who acts justly, and God will forgive the city, Jeremiah 5:1. Ezekiel hears that even Noah, Daniel and Job could only save themselves, Ezekiel 14:14, and that God searched for someone to "stand in the gap" and found no one, Ezekiel 22:30. Isaiah sees God amazed "that there was no one to intercede," so that "His own arm brought salvation," Isaiah 59:16. Isaiah 53:11-12 then describes the righteous Servant who "will justify many" and "made intercession for the transgressors."

The New Testament gathers these threads. Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7 call Abraham God's friend, and James 2:23 repeats it. Jesus tells His disciples, "I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you," John 15:15, the very logic of verse 17. Paul asks whether God is unjust and answers that He is the one who will "judge the world," Romans 3:5-6. Christ is the intercessor who "always lives to intercede," Hebrews 7:25, the righteous one who suffered "for the unrighteous," 1 Peter 3:18.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand the purpose of their election. Verse 19 says God chose Abraham so that he would teach his household to keep "the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just." Israel was to be a people of justice and righteousness, and the scene that follows shows what that looks like in their founder: a man who cares whether the innocent perish, and who appeals to God's own justice.

He also wanted Israel to trust the Judge. The coming destruction of Sodom could look arbitrary or excessive. This dialogue answers that fear in advance. God investigates before He acts, verse 21. He would spare the whole city for ten righteous people. When the fire falls in chapter 19, the reader knows it is not because God was careless with the innocent.

Third, Moses meant Israel to see what a mediator is. Abraham is the first in a line that runs through Moses, Samuel and the prophets. God takes His friend into His confidence precisely so that he can speak to God about what God has revealed. Prayer here is not persuading a reluctant deity but taking part, by invitation, in God's own work.

Finally, the passage gives Israel a pattern of reverent boldness. Abraham calls himself "dust and ashes," yet presses his case six times. The first hearers were meant to learn that humility and boldness in prayer are not opposites.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The dialogue itself is a unique event. God does not promise to hold a bargaining conversation over every city, and the specific numbers, fifty down to ten, are not a formula for how many righteous people will save a community. Later Scripture shows that God sometimes says the time for such intercession is past, Jeremiah 7:16 and 15:1.

What the passage does commend is a pattern of prayer that the New Testament makes prescriptive. Believers are told to offer "petitions, prayers, intercessions" for everyone, 1 Timothy 2:1, and that "the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail," James 5:16. Abraham's prayer shows the right grounds: he appeals not to his own merit but to God's character, and he prays for people outside the covenant.

The passage also describes God's disclosure of His plans to a chosen servant, which Amos 3:7 generalises to the prophets. Believers now receive that confidence in Christ, John 15:15, not in private revelations about coming judgments but in the gospel that tells them what God is doing in the world.

debates.question: Did Abraham change God's mind, or was he drawn into God's own purpose?

views.label: Genuine intercession that moves God to relent
views.case: The text reads as a real dialogue in which God responds to each request, and the outcome, the promise to spare the city for ten, is stated as God's answer to Abraham. Elsewhere God relents in response to prayer, Exodus 32:14. On this view God ordains prayer as a true means by which His mercy is expressed, and intercession really matters in history.

views.label: God leading Abraham to discover His own heart
views.case: God initiates the conversation by revealing His plan, verse 17, precisely because He intends Abraham to plead. He never refuses a request and never names a lower limit Himself. The descending questions teach Abraham, and the reader, how far God's mercy already extends, rather than altering an unchanging God.

debates.bearing: Both affirm that God's justice is never in doubt and that intercession matters. The text holds together God's settled purpose and a real, responsive conversation, and it encourages bold prayer that rests on who God is.

debates.question: Why does Abraham stop at ten?

views.label: Abraham thought ten was surely safe
views.case: Lot's household alone, with his wife, daughters, sons-in-law and perhaps others, might come close to ten. Abraham may have stopped because he believed the number would be found, and saw no need to go further. Chapter 19 shows how wrong that hope was: only four are brought out, and one of them is lost.

views.label: Abraham sensed the limit of what he should ask
views.case: The growing deference of his prefaces, "May the Lord not be angry," suggests he felt he had reached the edge of what he could ask. Ten may also represent the smallest meaningful community; later Jewish practice made ten the minimum for congregational prayer. Asking for fewer would be asking God to spare a city that was in effect wholly wicked.

views.label: The number matters less than the principle
views.case: Some read the stopping point as the narrative's way of leaving the question open. God has shown He will spare the many for the few; chapter 19 then shows Him doing something even more precise, rescuing the few from among the many, Genesis 19:29.

debates.bearing: The text does not tell us Abraham's reason, and it does not need to. God never set the limit, and in the end He did more than Abraham asked: He could not find ten, but He remembered Abraham and brought Lot out, and He waited to act until Lot was safe, Genesis 19:22.

debates.question: What does God mean by "I will go down to see," verse 21?

views.label: Language of judicial process
views.case: God does not need information, but He acts as a just judge who investigates before sentencing. The same phrasing appears at Babel, where "the LORD came down to see the city," Genesis 11:5. The language shows that God's judgments are never hasty or based on hearsay.

views.label: God's real engagement in history
views.case: Others stress that the text presents God as personally involved, coming near to examine what is happening, rather than ruling from a distance. The two angels who go on to Sodom in verse 22 are the means of that investigation, and what they meet at Lot's door, Genesis 19:4-9, is the evidence.

debates.bearing: Both readings guard against the idea that God judges carelessly. God knows all things, but He chooses to show His justice in a way people can see and verify, which is exactly the assurance Abraham asks for in verse 25.

study.originalLanguages:
The word the BSB renders "chosen" in verse 19 is yada, to know. God says, literally, "I have known him." The same verb describes God's covenant choice of Israel, "Only you have I known from all the families of the earth," Amos 3:2. Two verses later God says of Sodom, "If not, I will find out," verse 21, again literally "I will know." God knows Abraham in choosing love and will know Sodom in judicial scrutiny. In the next chapter the men of Sodom demand to "know" the visitors, Genesis 19:5, the same verb in a violent sense. The two chapters move through three kinds of knowing.

Verse 19 sets out the goal of Abraham's election as tsedaqah umishpat, "what is right and just," literally righteousness and justice. The pair becomes a summary of what God requires and what God does, Jeremiah 9:24 and Psalm 89:14. It is therefore striking that verse 20 introduces Sodom with a word that sounds very close to tsedaqah. The "outcry," tseaqah in verse 21 and its variant zeaqah in verse 20, is the scream of those who suffer injustice. Isaiah 5:7 later plays on the same pair: God "looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress." Where righteousness should be, there is an outcry instead.

Abraham's first question in verse 23 uses the verb saphah, "sweep away." It is a strong word for destruction that carries off everything together. The angels use it twice in the next chapter when they warn Lot, "or you will be swept away," Genesis 19:15 and 19:17. The very fate Abraham feared for the righteous is the fate from which Lot is dragged.

In verse 24 Abraham asks whether God will "not spare the place." The verb is nasa, which means to lift or carry, and in relation to sin it means to forgive, to bear it away. It stands in the confession of Exodus 34:7, "forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin." Abraham is asking God to bear with the city, to carry its guilt for the sake of the righteous in it. The word reaches toward a later idea: sin being carried by one on behalf of others, Isaiah 53:11-12.

The exclamation chalilah, "Far be it," verse 25, is built on a root meaning profane or common. It says, in effect, that such a thing would be a profanation, unworthy of God. Samuel uses it of ceasing to pray, 1 Samuel 12:23, and Elihu of God doing wrong, Job 34:10. Abraham uses it twice in one verse, a cry of horror at the thought that the Judge could act unjustly.

The title "Judge of all the earth," verse 25, pairs the participle shophet with the question "do what is right," ya'aseh mishpat, literally "do justice." Judge and justice come from the same root. Abraham is saying that the one whose very title is Judge cannot fail to do the thing His title names. Psalm 94:2 calls on "the Judge of the earth" in the same way.

Abraham calls himself "dust and ashes," afar va'efer, verse 27, a pair that rhymes in Hebrew. Dust recalls his origin, Genesis 2:7 and 3:19; ashes may recall what is left after burning, the very fate Sodom faces. Job uses the same pair in his humiliation and his repentance, Job 30:19 and 42:6.

Finally, verse 22 carries an ancient scribal note. Jewish tradition lists it among a small number of places where the scribes are said to have adjusted the wording out of reverence, and that original reading would have been "the LORD remained standing before Abraham." Whether or not that tradition is correct, the received text presents Abraham in the posture of a servant, and later Scripture remembers Moses in the same posture, standing "before Him in the breach," Psalm 106:23.

typology.type: A whole city spared for the sake of the righteous few, Genesis 18:26-32
typology.fulfillment: God agrees that the presence of righteous people could protect a whole city from judgment. The principle is reversed and fulfilled in Christ. In Sodom not even ten could be found, and Scripture confesses "there is no one righteous, not even one," Romans 3:10. God therefore provides His own righteous one, and through "the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous," Romans 5:19. The escalation is enormous: not ten for a city but one for a multitude from every nation. The type falls short because Abraham's ten would only delay judgment; Christ's righteousness removes it.

typology.type: Abraham standing before the LORD as intercessor, Genesis 18:22
typology.fulfillment: Abraham stands between God and a doomed city, pleading on the ground of God's justice. Christ is the fulfilment of every such mediator. He "made intercession for the transgressors," Isaiah 53:12, prayed for those crucifying Him, Luke 23:34, and now "always lives to intercede" for those who come to God through Him, Hebrews 7:25. Where Abraham asked for mercy and hoped the numbers would be enough, Christ pleads on the basis of His own finished sacrifice, and His prayer is never refused. Abraham could not save Sodom; Christ saves completely.

typology.type: The friend of God who is told His plans, Genesis 18:17
typology.fulfillment: God will not hide His purpose from Abraham because Abraham is His chosen friend, Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23. Jesus extends that friendship to all His disciples: "I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you," John 15:15. The escalation is that friendship with God is no longer the privilege of one patriarch but of every believer in Christ. Abraham was told of judgment coming on a city; believers are told of the whole counsel of salvation, revealed in the Son.

typology.type: The search for a righteous remnant in a doomed city
typology.fulfillment: The dialogue leaves the reader asking whether ten righteous will be found, and chapter 19 answers no. The prophets repeat the search, Jeremiah 5:1 and Ezekiel 22:30, always with the same result. Isaiah 59:16 draws the conclusion: God saw there was no one to intercede, "so His own arm brought salvation." The New Testament names that arm. God made Christ "who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God," 2 Corinthians 5:21. The remnant God could not find, He supplies.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first through its question. Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do right, and whether He will sweep away the righteous with the wicked. The cross is the place where that question receives its deepest answer. There the righteous one was swept away with the wicked, "numbered with the transgressors," Isaiah 53:12, not by accident but by design, so that the wicked could be treated as righteous. Paul says God did this "to demonstrate His righteousness," so as "to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus," Romans 3:26. Abraham could not imagine God allowing the righteous to suffer with the wicked; at Calvary God chose it, and it was just because the righteous one bore the penalty willingly.

It leads to Christ through its principle. God would spare the many for the sake of the few. Abraham hoped for fifty, then settled for ten, and even ten could not be found. Scripture's verdict is that "there is no one righteous, not even one," Romans 3:10. The gospel answer is that God provided one. "Just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous," Romans 5:19. Caiaphas said more than he knew when he declared "it is better for you that one man die for the people," John 11:50.

It leads to Christ through its intercessor. Abraham stood before the LORD for a city that did not know he was praying. Jesus prayed for those who did not know what they were doing, Luke 23:34. He prayed for Peter before Peter fell, Luke 22:31-32. He prayed not only for His disciples but "for those who will believe in Me through their message," John 17:20. And He now "is interceding for us" at God's right hand, Romans 8:34. Abraham's prayer had limits, fifty down to ten, and it was bounded by his fear of angering God. Christ's intercession has no such limits, because He pleads His own blood.

It leads to Christ through friendship. God confides in Abraham because He has chosen him to teach righteousness and justice. Jesus calls His disciples friends and makes known to them all He heard from the Father, John 15:15. The friendship Abraham enjoyed as a singular privilege is offered to all who belong to Christ.

The link should not be forced. Abraham is not a disguised picture of Christ at every point; his bargaining, his fear and his limits are what make him unlike Christ. But the New Testament reads the whole Old Testament search for a righteous intercessor as fulfilled in Jesus, and this passage is where that search begins.
study.god:
The passage shows God as a Judge who is just in a way that can be examined. He does not simply announce destruction. He says He will "go down to see," verse 21, and He allows His chosen friend to question Him on whether He will act rightly. God is not threatened by the question "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" He welcomes it, because the answer is yes. His justice is not arbitrary will but a character that can be appealed to and relied upon, Psalm 89:14.

He is merciful beyond what is asked. At every stage Abraham asks, and God grants without hesitation or counter-offer. God never says "no," never names a lower bound, never rebukes Abraham for asking again. The pattern shows a God who is "slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion," Exodus 34:6, and who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 18:23. If ten righteous had been found, the city would have stood.

He is a God who reveals. "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" verse 17. God is under no obligation to explain Himself, yet He chooses to bring His friend into His counsel. Amos 3:7 says He "does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets." The God of the Bible is a speaking, disclosing God, whose purposes are made known to those He has chosen.

He honours prayer. God initiates the conversation by revealing His plan, and He then responds to Abraham's requests. The passage holds together what theology often struggles to hold: God's settled purpose and His real responsiveness to the prayers of His people. Abraham does not overrule God, but neither is he talking to a wall.

He keeps His covenant purposes in view even in judgment. God's reason for telling Abraham is rooted in the promise that "all the nations of the earth will be blessed" through him, verse 18. Even as He prepares to judge one city of the nations, God is thinking about blessing the nations through Abraham's line.

He holds justice and mercy together without compromising either. Abraham's argument is that sparing the righteous is what justice requires, and that sparing the wicked for their sake is what mercy allows. God agrees on both counts. The ultimate reconciliation of the two is not reached here. It waits for the cross, where God shows Himself both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:26.

For worship, the passage teaches believers to pray with confidence grounded in God's character, to care for those outside the covenant, and to trust that the Judge of all the earth will always do what is right, even when we cannot see it.

crossReferences.note: The Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets. Genesis 18:17 is the first instance of that principle: God will not hide from Abraham what He is about to do, and Genesis 20:7 then calls Abraham a prophet.

Abraham 'was called a friend of God,' a title first given in Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7. Genesis 18:17 shows that friendship in action: God treats Abraham as someone with whom He shares His counsel, not merely as a servant who receives orders.

Jesus says He no longer calls His disciples servants, because a servant does not know his master's business, but friends, because He has made known everything He learned from the Father. The logic of Genesis 18:17 is extended to every disciple.

God looked for justice and righteousness in His vineyard but heard a cry of distress. The same contrast appears between Genesis 18:19, where Abraham is to teach righteousness and justice, and 18:20-21, where an outcry rises from Sodom. Isaiah applies the pattern to Israel itself.

God tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem's streets for a single person who acts justly, and He will forgive the city. Abraham began at fifty and stopped at ten; Jeremiah's search goes down to one, and even one cannot be found.

God searched for someone to stand in the gap on behalf of the land so He would not destroy it, but found no one. Abraham stood in that gap for Sodom. Ezekiel shows that the role Abraham filled had become empty in Israel's own day.

God would have destroyed Israel, 'had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach.' Moses repeats Abraham's posture of Genesis 18:22, standing before the LORD, and succeeds in turning back wrath from his people.

God saw that there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation. The failed search of Genesis 18 and the prophets ends here, with God Himself supplying the righteousness and intercession no human could provide.

Through the obedience of one man the many are made righteous. Abraham asked whether a few righteous could save a city; Paul announces that one righteous man, Christ, brings justification and life to a multitude.

Christ is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them. Abraham's intercession was limited and ended when the LORD departed; Christ's never ends.

When God destroyed the cities, He remembered Abraham and brought Lot out. Ten righteous were not found, but Abraham's prayer was not wasted. God answered the heart of his plea, that the righteous not be swept away with the wicked.

Paul asks whether God is unjust to inflict wrath and answers, 'Certainly not! In that case, how could God judge the world?' He assumes Abraham's conviction in Genesis 18:25 that the Judge of all the earth must do what is right.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapters of Genesis God has been a Judge. He judged the serpent, the man and the woman in Genesis 3, Cain in Genesis 4, and the whole corrupt earth in the flood, Genesis 6:5-7. In each case the question hovered: how can God judge a sinful world and still keep His promise to bless it? The flood showed that God could preserve a righteous family through judgment, 2 Peter 2:5. Genesis 18 asks a harder question: could the righteous few preserve the wicked many?

Abraham's role here is the role of his whole family. He was chosen so that "all the nations of the earth will be blessed" through him, verse 18, and here the blessing takes the form of prayer for a Canaanite city. Israel would inherit that calling, to be a kingdom of priests standing between God and the nations. Moses, Samuel and the prophets would take up Abraham's posture before God, sometimes turning wrath aside, sometimes being told the time for pleading was past.

The chapter also sets up a search that runs through the rest of the Old Testament. Ten righteous were not found in Sodom. Jeremiah was sent to find one in Jerusalem. Ezekiel heard that God found no one to stand in the gap. The question left hanging at the end of Genesis 18, whether there would ever be enough righteousness to save a city, becomes the question of whether there will ever be enough to save the world.

The New Testament gives the answer in Christ. He is the righteous one for whose sake God spares a multitude, and He is the intercessor who pleads for transgressors. At the cross the Judge of all the earth did right in the most surprising way, by bearing the judgment Himself. God shows that He is able "to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus," Romans 3:26.

The story ends in a city unlike Sodom. The new Jerusalem has no outcry in it: "no more death or mourning or crying or pain," Revelation 21:4. Its people are not a remnant of ten but "a multitude too large to count," Revelation 7:9, all made righteous in the one righteous Man. And the friendship God offered Abraham becomes the whole life of the city, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," Revelation 21:3.

quiz.q: What is the great question at the heart of Abraham's plea?

options.text: Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?
options.note: Abraham stakes his whole appeal on God's perfect justice.

options.text: Will God spare Lot no matter what?
options.note: Lot is in view, but the explicit question is about God's justice for all.

options.text: Why does God allow evil cities to exist?
options.note: That is not the question the text raises here.

options.text: Can Abraham become more righteous than Sodom?
options.note: Abraham calls himself dust and ashes; the question is about God's justice, not his own merit.

quiz.q: On what basis does Abraham plead for Sodom?

options.text: On the presence of the righteous, asking God to spare the city for their sake.
options.note: He appeals to the righteous few within the wicked city.

options.text: On the argument that Sodom was not really that sinful.
options.note: He never disputes their guilt; he appeals to the righteous within.

options.text: On his own good works and standing before God.
options.note: He calls himself dust and ashes; his plea rests on the righteous, not himself.

options.text: On the claim that God has no right to judge.
options.note: He affirms God's right to judge; he appeals to God's justice and mercy.

quiz.q: Why does the LORD choose to tell Abraham His plans?

options.text: Because Abraham is chosen and through him the nations will be blessed.
options.note: God treats Abraham as a friend and covenant partner.

options.text: Because God needed Abraham's permission to act.
options.note: God confides in him as a friend, but does not require his permission.

options.text: Because Abraham had demanded to know.
options.note: God volunteers the information; Abraham does not demand it.

options.text: Because Abraham lived in Sodom.
options.note: Abraham lived at Mamre; it was Lot who lived in Sodom.

quiz.q: How far did the LORD agree to go in sparing the city?

options.text: He agreed to spare it for the sake of as few as ten righteous ones.
options.note: The dialogue descends from fifty to ten.

options.text: He agreed to spare it only if fifty righteous were found.
options.note: Fifty was the starting point; He went all the way down to ten.

options.text: He refused to spare it under any condition.
options.note: He repeatedly agreed to spare it for the righteous.

options.text: He promised to spare it for the sake of one righteous person.
options.note: The dialogue stops at ten, not one.

quiz.q: How does this scene point to Christ?

options.text: Where no righteous remnant is found, God provides one righteous One for whose sake many are spared.
options.note: Christ's righteousness justifies many, Romans 5.

options.text: It shows that cities can always save themselves by good citizens.
options.note: The deeper pointer is to the one righteous One, not civic virtue.

options.text: It teaches that judgment never actually falls.
options.note: Judgment does fall on Sodom; mercy is shown through the righteous.

options.text: It proves that intercession is pointless.
options.note: Abraham's intercession foreshadows Christ's effective intercession.

questions: God confided in Abraham as a friend before acting. What does it mean to you that God draws His people close rather than keeping them at a distance?
Abraham interceded boldly yet humbly, calling himself 'dust and ashes.' Who is God laying on your heart to pray for, and how can you plead for them?
Abraham anchored his prayer in God's character: 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' How does trusting God's justice help you when the world seems unfair?
God was willing to spare a whole city for the sake of a righteous few. How does that shape the way you see the value of faithful believers in a hard place?
In Christ, God provides the one righteous One for whose sake many are spared. How does that truth give you confidence to draw near to God today?

translationNotes.note: Outcry translates a word used for the cry of the oppressed; Sodom's sin has provoked a cry that reaches heaven.
Far be it from You renders an idiom of horror at the unthinkable; Abraham appeals to God's own character, not merely to an outcome.
The Judge of all the earth uses a verb meaning to judge, govern, and vindicate; it affirms God's sovereign right and perfect rightness in judgment.
